statement: Particle geometry in the diffusion-reaction model affects radial reactant transport and adsorption kinetics.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Higher dimensional reactant diffusion in cylindrical and spherical particles reduces the exposure needed for complete penetration compared to slabs.

statement: Particle geometry affects intraparticle reactant transport in diffusion-reaction modeling.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Different porous substrate shapes map directly to specific application-relevant particle models like slabs for membranes and spheres for catalysts.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Gordon et al. showed required reactant exposure scales quadratically with aspect ratio in high aspect ratio features.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: In spherical geometry, gas demand decreases toward the particle center as shell volume decreases.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: In the literature, the shape factor is determined as the external surface area divided by the particle volume, which is then multiplied by the particle radius R.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Shape factors for different geometries alter intraparticle diffusion and surface coverage profiles.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Reactant consumption profiles vary according to the geometric shape factor of the porous particle.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Equation (1) gives the diffusion-reaction equation for volumetric reactant number density over time across particle geometries using shape factor s.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: In this work we use the common concept that the reactant exposure (Pa s) is the partial pressure multiplied by the reactant exposure time.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: In the eqn (1), the symbol s is the shape factor with a relationship s = a - 1, where factor a has values of one, two and three for a slab, cylinder and sphere, respectively.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: The effective diffusion coefficient (De, m2 s−1), is derived from the gas phase diffusion coefficient in porous materials, consisting of both molecular diffusion and Knudsen diffusion factors.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Equation (2) expresses the Bosanquet relation combining molecular and Knudsen diffusion coefficients into the overall gas-phase diffusion coefficient.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Molecular diffusion is assumed negligible relative to Knudsen diffusion because pore dimensions are much smaller than the mean free path.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Equation (3) equates the overall gas diffusion coefficient to the Knudsen diffusion coefficient under pure Knudsen flow.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Equation (4) calculates the effective diffusion coefficient in porous media from the Knudsen diffusion coefficient scaled by porosity over tortuosity.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Equation (5) determines the effective diffusion coefficient using kinetic gas theory parameters, pore diameter, porosity, and tortuosity.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Equation (6) defines the 1D diffusion-reaction partial differential equation for a slab geometry (s = 0).
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Equation (7) defines the radial diffusion-reaction partial differential equation for a cylinder geometry (s = 1).
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Equation (8) defines the radial diffusion-reaction partial differential equation for a spherical geometry (s = 2).
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Equation (9) gives the rate of change of surface coverage according to irreversible single-site Langmuir adsorption kinetics.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Equation (10) specifies the initial condition of zero surface coverage throughout the particle domain at t = 0.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Equation (11) specifies the initial condition of zero reactant number density throughout the particle at t = 0.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Equation (12) sets the Dirichlet boundary condition fixing reactant number density at the particle surface (r = 0) to np0.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Equation (13) sets the Neumann boundary condition requiring zero radial flux of reactant at the particle center (r = R).
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: The spatial domain of the radius was discretized typically using 300 points.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: The penetration depth (r_{0=1/2}) in Fig. 2(a) and (b) was 177, 133 and 114 µm for the spherical (s = 2), cylindrical (s = 1) and slab (s = 0) geometries, respectively.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: For a constant exposure, the ALD coating penetration depth increases in the sequence slab < cylinder < sphere.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Reactant number density decreases linearly with depth in slab geometry due to 1D diffusion, but exhibits curved profiles in cylindrical geometry due to 2D diffusion.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: In spherical particles, the available deposition area per shell volume shrinks towards the particle centre, allowing deeper penetration.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Particle shape factor alters penetration depth but has no significant effect on the front slope or shape of the surface coverage profile.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: The value for the penetration depth (r_{\theta=1/2}) is determined as the position where the surface coverage \theta = 0.5.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Full penetration at 1e5 Pa s is achieved for R <= 275 µm (sphere), R <= 225 µm (cylinder), and R <= 161 µm (slab).

statement: Lower porosity increases diffusion resistance, which reduces reactant penetration depth.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Higher tortuosity-to-porosity ratio tau/epsilon restricts diffusion, causing the penetration depths of slab and sphere to converge.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Increasing the reactant molar mass lowers the thermal velocity, decreasing reactant penetration depth.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Higher areal saturation density sigma of deposited atoms increases reactant consumption per unit area and reduces penetration depth.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Increasing surface area to pore volume ratio s_bar provides more adsorption sites per unit volume, reducing the penetration depth.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Varying initial sticking coefficient beta_0 has no significant effect on the average penetration depth.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Under reactant depletion, lower sticking probability reduces surface adsorption rate, slightly increasing penetration.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Penetration depth increases linearly with pore diameter due to enhanced Knudsen diffusion.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Increasing pore diameter from 10 to 40 nm doubles penetration depth for a slab and increases it 2.5-fold for a sphere.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Decreasing sticking probability broadens the adsorption front, decreasing the profile front slope.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: In spherical geometry reactant propagation varies radially due to convergent geometry, whereas slab propagation is uniform.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Increasing the specific surface area raises adsorption site density per volume, reducing the coating penetration depth.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Increasing pore diameter raises the Knudsen diffusion coefficient, enhancing diffusion and increasing penetration depth.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Prior studies reported that increasing deposition temperature reduces coating penetration depth.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: With fixed initial reactant number density, penetration depth increases with temperature due to faster diffusion and reaction rates.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: When fixing partial pressure, initial reactant number density and achieved penetration depth decrease with temperature.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Less reactant is required to coat spherical and cylindrical particles than slab geometries due to converging geometry.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: At fixed exposure, increasing specific surface area decreases coating penetration depth.
author: 10.1039_d3cp05639b

statement: Increasing pore diameter at fixed exposure leads to decreased coating penetration depth.

statement: Increasing pore volume increases the ALD coating penetration depth.
